docs.title: Project overview
docs.text:
SongList Backend is a Django + Django REST Framework API for running a multi‑tenant music service. It powers tenants (venues), users, playlists, song catalogues, and subscription billing.

  • Tenants – each tenant represents a venue or organisation.
  • Users – listener, admin, and super‑admin roles with JWT authentication.
  • Music data – songs, genres, playlists, tenant–song links, and song requests.
  • Payments – Razorpay‑backed subscriptions so tenants can become premium.

The backend is designed for production use:

  • Testing – a central tests/ package built on pytest, factory_boy, and DRF’s APIClient.
  • Optimisation & monitoring – optional request profilers (Silk, PyInstrument), New Relic APM, and Locust load tests.
  • Deployment – Docker and docker‑compose, GitHub Actions CI/CD, and an AWS EC2 host.

docs.title: How to use this documentation
docs.text:
If you’re new, start with:

  1. Testing: How we test the project with pytest, fixtures/factories, and coverage reporting.

  2. Optimization: How we profile performance (Silk/PyInstrument/New Relic), prevent query inefficiencies, and run load tests with Locust.

  3. Deployment: The end-to-end deployment flow from GitHub Actions to GHCR and AWS EC2, plus the Docker Compose runtime stack (including Nginx/SSL).

You can also browse the source code on GitHub at: - https://github.com/riddhima-gkmit/SongList-Backend.git

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SongList Backend uses a fully automated CI/CD pipeline built on GitHub Actions. Every push to the main or ci-cd branches (or merged pull request into main) triggers a test run, a Docker image build, and deployment to an AWS EC2 instance.

The production runtime is a Docker Compose stack with multiple services: a Django/Gunicorn web server, PostgreSQL, Redis, a Celery worker, and Celery Beat, plus Nginx and a helper Certbot container. Nginx acts as a reverse proxy and serves static files directly.

docs.title: Tools for CI/CD - Docker
docs.text:
• Docker: Containerizing the application for consistency.
  • Docker Compose: Orchestrating our multi-container architecture.
  • GitHub Actions: Primary CI/CD automation platform.
  • GHCR: Storing and managing our Docker images.
  • uv: Fast Python package manager for dependencies.
  • Gunicorn: Production WSGI server running our Django app.
  • New Relic: Provides robust application performance monitoring in production.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step Detail 1 Checkout repository actions/checkout@v4 2 Install uv pip install uv 3 Set up Python 3.13 actions/setup-python@v5 4 Install dependencies uv sync --frozen (locked versions) 5 Run Pytest uv run pytest --tb=short -v — full suite against Postgres + Redis service containers

Gate: The build-and-deploy job only runs if this job succeeds.

docs.title: Build & Push Job (build-and-deploy)
docs.text: Requires packages: write permission to push to GHCR.

docs.title: Build steps
docs.text: # Step Action 1 Login to GHCR docker/login-action@v3 using GITHUB_TOKEN 2 Extract metadata docker/metadata-action@v5 → produces sha-{SHA} and latest tags 3 Set up Docker Buildx docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 4 Build & push docker/build-push-action@v6 with registry cache and inline cache

docs.title: Deploy to EC2 (inline script)
docs.text:
After the image is pushed, the workflow SSHs into EC2 (appleboy/ssh-action@v1, 600s timeout) and runs an inline Bash script. All GitHub Secrets are written into a .env file before docker compose is invoked.

The script is idempotent — every deploy:

  1. Ensures /opt/songlist exists and is owned by the deploy user.
  2. Clones the repository on first deploy, or runs git fetch + git reset --hard origin/<branch> on subsequent deploys.
  3. Writes .env from GitHub Secrets (database, Redis, email, Razorpay, New Relic, etc.).
  4. Logs in to GHCR using a personal access token (GHCR_PAT).
  5. Pulls the latest image:
docker pull ghcr.io/<owner>/songlist-backend:latest
  1. Starts or updates the Docker Compose stack:
docker compose up -d --no-build
  1. Cleans up dangling images:
docker image prune -f

docs.title: Runtime stack (Docker Compose)
docs.text:
On EC2, docker compose uses the docker-compose.yml file in the repo root. The main services are:

Service Description web Django + Gunicorn, started via newrelic-admin run-program, serves the API on port 8000 inside the compose network celery-worker Celery worker process, also wrapped in newrelic-admin run-program celery-beat Celery Beat scheduler, wrapped in newrelic-admin run-program db PostgreSQL 16 with postgres_data volume and pg_isready healthcheck redis Redis 7 used for cache and Celery broker/result backend nginx Reverse proxy listening on ports 80/443, serving /static and /media and proxying to web:8000 certbot Helper container for obtaining/renewing Let’s Encrypt certificates (invoked manually)

The Nginx config lives at deploy/nginx/conf.d/songlist.conf and:

  • Serves the ACME HTTP-01 challenge from /var/www/certbot.
  • Serves /static/ and /media/ from the static_data and media_data volumes.
  • Proxies all other traffic to the web service.

docs.title: DNS, Security Groups, and SSL
docs.text:
In production there is typically some surrounding infrastructure in front of the Docker stack:

  1. Configure DNS
  2. Point a domain like api.example.com (A or CNAME record) to your EC2 instance, or to a load balancer in front of it.

  3. Once DNS propagates, requests to that hostname will reach your Nginx container on the EC2 host.

  4. Lock down network access (security groups / firewall)

  5. Allow inbound 80/tcp and 443/tcp from the internet so HTTP/HTTPS traffic can reach Nginx.
  6. Optionally, restrict 22/tcp (SSH) so only a bastion host or trusted IP ranges can connect.

docs.title: Running Certbot manually
docs.text:
The certbot service in docker-compose.yml is intentionally minimal and does not auto-provision certificates. A typical manual flow on EC2 is:

  1. Verify Nginx is serving the ACME challenge path

  2. Ensure the stack is up and that Nginx is serving /.well-known/acme-challenge/ from /var/www/certbot as configured in deploy/nginx/conf.d/songlist.conf.

  3. Request a certificate with Certbot

  4. Run Certbot inside the certbot container, pointing it at the same webroot:

```bash docker compose run --rm certbot certonly \ --webroot -w /var/www/certbot \ -d api.example.com \ --email you@example.com \ --agree-tos --no-eff-email

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
• django-silk: HTTP and SQL profiler integrated into Django. Use when you want to inspect per-request SQL, spot N+1 queries, and see slow views locally or on a staging server (/silk/).

  • pyinstrument: Sampling profiler for Python call stacks. Use when a request is slow but not obviously DB-bound and you need to see which functions and lines consume most wall time.

  • New Relic APM: Production-grade monitoring. Use when you need real-time performance charts, error traces, slow-transaction breakdowns, and database time in your live environment.

  • Locust: HTTP load-testing tool. Use when you want to simulate concurrent listeners/admins (e.g. browsing playlists, requesting songs) and measure throughput, latency, and failure rates.

docs.title: Query Optimization Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use select_related for single-object relations Apply it to foreign key / one-to-one relationships (e.g. requester, tenant, subscription, song) when serializing lists. This pushes joins into a single SQL query and avoids N+1 on detail fields.

  2. Use prefetch_related for collections For many-to-many and reverse foreign key relationships (e.g. playlist songs, tenant users), use prefetch_related to fetch related rows in a small, fixed number of queries.

  3. Annotate instead of per-row .count() For things like song_count per genre or user_count per tenant, prefer annotate(Count(...)) on the queryset rather than calling .count() inside a serializer or property.

  4. Project only what you need When returning large lists, use .only() or .values() / .values_list() if you truly only need a subset of fields.

docs.title: Optimization Techniques in SongList Backend
docs.text:
We use several layers of optimization:

  • Database indexing
  • Primary keys (UUIDs) and common filter fields (e.g. tenant_id, deleted_at, status) are indexed by default or via model constraints.

  • Where possible, queries are written to align with these indices (e.g. filtering on deleted_at__isnull=True rather than scanning soft-deleted rows).

  • N+1 query prevention

  • List endpoints are progressively being updated to use select_related/prefetch_related for related objects accessed in serializers.

  • Properties that compute counts (user_count, genre song counts, etc.) should be moved to queryset annotations to avoid per-row queries.

  • Redis caching

  • Frequently accessed, read-heavy lists (such as tenant songs or genres) are cached in Redis behind helper functions and cache keys.

  • Cache invalidation hooks are used on create/update/delete operations for those resources.

  • Background work via Celery

  • Non-critical and heavier tasks (email notifications, payment/plan reconciliation, etc.) are pushed to Celery workers so that API responses stay fast for end users.

docs.title: Tools for TDD
docs.text:
• pytest: Primary test runner for this codebase.
  • pytest-django: Django integration for pytest (sets up the test DB + Django environment).
  • factory-boy: Generates realistic model instances from factories in tests/factories/.
  • pytest-cov: Produces coverage reports (HTML in htmlcov/).
  • Mocks and stubs: Used mainly to prevent external network calls (e.g., Razorpay) from running during tests.

docs.title: Project Test Structure
docs.text:
• tests/conftest.py: shared fixtures (including authenticated DRF clients).
  • tests/factories/: factory classes for model creation (e.g., UserFactory, TenantFactory, PaymentTransactionFactory).
  • tests/tenant/: tenant models/serializers/views tests.
  • tests/payment/: payment models/serializers/views tests.

docs.title: Example Test Case
docs.text:
This is a minimal example using an actual factory from this project:

import pytest
from tests.factories.tenant_factory import TenantFactory

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_tenant_is_active_by_default():
    tenant = TenantFactory()
    assert tenant.is_active is True

docs.title: Executing Test Cases
docs.text:
# Run all tests
uv run pytest

# Run a specific area
uv run pytest tests/tenant/
uv run pytest tests/payment/

# Run tests matching a keyword
uv run pytest -k "payment"

docs.title: Terminal commands
docs.text:
# Run tests with coverage enabled
uv run pytest --cov=.

# Generate detailed HTML report
uv run pytest --cov=. --cov-report=html
